blocks.text: The **Internet** is a worldwide network of **interconnected networks**. It carries web pages, email, files, calls and many other services. The basic rules computers follow to talk to each other come from **TCP/IP**.

blocks.title: Not an acronym
blocks.text: 'Internet' is not a short form of anything. The phrase 'interconnected networks' only describes its meaning.

blocks.title: Origins
rows: Advanced Research Projects Agency Network; operational in 1969 and a major precursor of today's Internet
On 1 January 1983 ARPANET adopted TCP/IP, often called the birth of the modern Internet

blocks.title: People to remember
rows: Co-designed TCP/IP; widely called the Fathers of the Internet
Developed the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), which prevents loops in Ethernet networks; popularly called the Mother of the Internet

blocks.title: India and early access
rows: Formally launched on 15 August 1995; pre-launch service began on 14 August
Pioneered commercial public packet-data service; calling it the first modern ISP is a simplification
The usual exam answer for India's first political party with a website; reported launch years vary

blocks.text: ARPA to ARPANET (1969), TCP/IP milestone (1983), public Internet service in India (1995).

**WWW** means World Wide Web, also called the **Web** or **W3**. It is a system of linked pages and resources accessed through the Internet. The Internet is the network infrastructure; the Web is just **one service** that runs on it.

blocks.title: Birth of the Web
items: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the Web while working at CERN
First browser, server and website working (by end of 1990), hosted on his NeXT computer
Public announcement of the Web project on the Internet

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: Its English name is European Organization for Nuclear Research; the acronym comes from its historical French name
World Wide Web Consortium; develops open web standards
Created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN to explain the WWW project

blocks.text: Do not mix up the 1989 proposal, the 1990 working system and the 1991 public announcement. Also, CERN is the institution while info.cern.ch is the website address.

blocks.title: Pages, sites and links
rows: A document displayed by a browser
A collection of related pages and resources
Clickable text, image, icon or button leading to another resource or a place within the same page

blocks.text: HTML is a **markup language**, not a programming language.

blocks.title: HTTP and old web programs
rows: Hypertext Transfer Protocol; exchanges web requests and responses
Small Java programs embedded in web pages
Supported animation and multimedia; not a generic name for every small web program. Adobe ended general Flash Player support on 31 December 2020

blocks.title: BOM and DOM
rows: Browser Object Model: the browser-window facilities, with window as the main global object
Document Object Model: the page's structure and elements, reached through window.document

blocks.text: HTML = structure, CSS = style, JavaScript = behaviour, HTTP = communication, hyperlink = navigation.

A **browser** is a client application that requests web resources and displays pages. A **search engine** is a different thing: a service for finding information. Browsers open websites directly from URLs, while some Internet services can also work through other apps.

blocks.title: The first browser
rows: Combined browsing with page editing; later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion with the Web itself

blocks.title: Mosaic and Lynx
rows: Developed by Marc Andreessen, Eric Bina and their team at the University of Illinois; made graphical browsing widely popular
Earlier graphical browsers existed, so Mosaic was not the first graphical browser

blocks.title: Netscape to Firefox
items: Open-source Mozilla project began (Mozilla was an internal Netscape name)

blocks.text: AOL acquired Netscape in 1999 but did not originally create Navigator. Also, Firefox is another name for the red panda, but the browser logo shows a fox.

blocks.title: Major browsers
rows: Launched in 2004; 'Universal Control' is not a verified standard expansion

blocks.title: Microsoft Edge and Internet Explorer
items: The original Edge shipped with Windows 10
Some services, such as Teams web, stopped supporting IE 11, but that was not its overall retirement
IE 11 desktop support ended on certain Windows 10 editions
**Tor** uses onion routing for privacy and can access ordinary websites as well as .onion services.
Do not treat the organisation's founding year (2006) as the browser's launch year.
Browser speed depends on the device, the connection and the page.

blocks.title: Quick match
blocks.text: Safari = Apple, Firefox = Mozilla, Edge = Microsoft, Epic = Hidden Reflex, UC = UCWeb, Chrome = Google.

In **open-source** software, the source code is available for inspection, modification and distribution under its license. Open-source browsers include Firefox, Chromium, Waterfox, Basilisk, Pale Moon, Brave and Dooble.
Free-of-charge software is not necessarily open source. 'Open source' is about code access and licence, not price.

blocks.title: Plugin versus extension
rows: Adds a specialized capability or runtime to another program
Adds browser features such as translation, password management or content blocking

blocks.title: Historical plugin examples (not routinely supported by today's browsers)
items: Adobe Flash Player: animation and multimedia
QuickTime and RealPlayer: audio and video

blocks.title: Incognito and Tor
blocks.text: Incognito reduces local session traces; it does not make a person anonymous. Tor Browser routes traffic through relays and helps hide the source IP address, which improves privacy but cannot guarantee perfect anonymity.

blocks.title: Before and during early web search
items: Archie, created by Alan Emtage at McGill (early work 1989); indexed FTP file listings, not full web pages
Gopher, a menu-based information retrieval system and protocol, not a conventional web search engine
Yahoo began as a web directory by Jerry Yang and David Filo
Lycos, by Michael Mauldin at Carnegie Mellon University
AltaVista, an early major search service
Ask Jeeves company founded in 1996; website launched in 1997; later called Ask.com

blocks.title: Late 1990s and the 2000s
items: Google Inc., by Larry Page and Sergey Brin
AOL Search relaunch (AOL = America Online; the 1999 date is a relaunch, not the company's founding)
Baidu, a Chinese search company, founded
AltaVista acquired by Overture; Yahoo acquired Overture later that year

blocks.text: Distinguish a service's launch, a company's incorporation and an acquisition date. They are different events and often fall in different years.

sections.title: Search Tools and How Search Works

blocks.title: Other major services
rows: Video-sharing and video-search platform; founders Steve Chen, Chad Hurley and Jawed Karim; website registered on 14 February 2005 (not the same event as its later full public launch); later became part of Google
Microsoft's search service, introduced in 2009 after MSN Search and Live Search
Launched in 2009; a computational knowledge engine that calculates answers from curated data and algorithms rather than just listing links

blocks.title: How a search engine works
items: Crawler or spider discovers pages and fetches content
Index or database stores the analysed information
Query processing selects and ranks relevant results
Search interface takes the query and shows results

blocks.title: Search vocabulary
rows: Search Engine Optimization: improving content and technical accessibility for search
Search Engine Marketing: marketing through search platforms, commonly paid search advertising

blocks.text: A browser opens pages; a search engine helps you find them. Crawling finds content, indexing organises it, and serving returns results.

sections.title: Internet, Intranet, Extranet and Layers of the Web

blocks.title: Internet, Intranet and Extranet
rows: An organisation's private internal network or services
Controlled access to selected organisational resources for authorised outsiders, such as partners and suppliers

blocks.text: Inter = between, Intra = within, Extra = outside.

blocks.title: Layers of the web
items: Public content ordinary search engines can index
Content outside ordinary public search indexes
Part of the Deep Web needing special networks or software

blocks.title: What each layer holds
rows: Public news articles, Wikipedia pages, blogs, product pages and public video pages
Private email, banking dashboards, medical records, internal databases, private Dropbox files, PayPal account details and subscription-protected content
A specialized part of the Deep Web requiring special networks or software; Tor onion services are an example

items: A platform can have both public and private areas: a public Netflix introduction page may be indexed while the protected content is not.
The Dark Web is used for privacy and censorship resistance, but criminal misuse can include fraud, illicit markets and ransomware-related services.
Cryptocurrency or encryption alone does not define the Dark Web.
Fixed claims such as '4% Surface and 96% Deep' are not reliable universal measurements.

blocks.text: **URL** means Uniform Resource Locator. In the example **https://www.example.com/notes**, each part has a name. A URL may also include a port, a query or a fragment, so the simple 'protocol plus resource address' idea is only an introduction.

blocks.title: Parts of a URL
rows: How to talk to the resource
The last part of the domain

blocks.title: IP address
rows: Identifies a network interface for addressing and packet delivery
A device can have several addresses, and addresses may change
Lets multiple devices share one public address

blocks.text: An IP address is not always a permanent identity for one computer.

blocks.title: Protocols to remember
rows: Transmission Control Protocol: reliable, ordered delivery of a byte stream
Internet Protocol: addressing and packet delivery
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: web requests and responses
Domain Name System: looks up records such as IP addresses for domain names
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: gives clients IP addresses and network settings

blocks.text: DNS = name lookup (like a phone book), DHCP = address and settings configuration.

Internet traffic travels in **packets** over shared network links. Packets can take **different routes**, and IP packets can have **different lengths** (subject to protocol and link limits); they are not universally fixed at 64 bytes.

blocks.title: Packet switching versus circuit switching
rows: Shares network capacity among many users
Reserves a circuit or capacity for the communication

blocks.title: TCP/IP and hosts
rows: A suite of related protocols, not a single protocol
Requests a service; a browser is one kind of client
A program or system that provides a service

blocks.text: A server runs on a host, but not every host is a server. A browser is one kind of client, but it is not required for every Internet application.

blocks.title: Broadband connections
rows: Digital Subscriber Line over copper telephone lines

blocks.text: Traditional dial-up uses a telephone modem connection and is **not broadband**. Connection performance varies with technology and conditions.

**Cookies** are small records stored by the browser on the **client side**. A server can set one using **Set-Cookie**, and the browser sends the relevant cookies back in later requests. JavaScript can set some cookies too. They are used for sessions, preferences and shopping carts. Browser storage is not always a separate plain-text file per cookie.

blocks.title: Files, browsing and patches
rows: Your device to a remote system
A change to software that fixes bugs, security flaws or compatibility problems; being free is not part of its definition

blocks.title: Voice and chat
rows: Voice over Internet Protocol, also called IP telephony; carries voice as digital packets over IP networks (WhatsApp voice calls are an example); it is not simply broadcasting
Internet Relay Chat: real-time text conversations in channels and private messages

blocks.title: Login and access
rows: Verifies identity, using a password, OTP or biometrics
Determines the actions a user is permitted to do

blocks.title: Final exam check
blocks.text: A login name and password check is authentication. HTML builds page structure, a URL locates a resource, IP addresses support network delivery, DHCP assigns settings, Tor improves privacy, and a browser is never the same thing as a search engine.

revision: The Internet is a worldwide network of interconnected networks and is not an acronym; TCP/IP provides its basic rules.
ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) was operational in 1969; it adopted TCP/IP on 1 January 1983.
Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn co-designed TCP/IP; Radia Perlman developed STP and is called the Mother of the Internet.
Public Internet service in India was formally launched on 15 August 1995 (pre-launch on 14 August); ISP = Internet Service Provider.
Tim Berners-Lee proposed the Web in 1989 at CERN; 1990 first browser and site (info.cern.ch); 1991 public announcement; W3C founded 1994.
HTML = structure, CSS = style, JavaScript = behaviour, HTTP = communication, HTTPS = HTTP protected by TLS.
First browser: WorldWideWeb (1990, NeXT), later renamed Nexus; Mosaic (1993) made graphical browsing popular; Lynx (1992) is text-based.
Netscape Navigator 1994; Mozilla project 1998; AOL bought Netscape in 1999; Firefox 1.0 in 2004.
Safari = Apple (2003), Chrome = Google (2008), Edge = Microsoft, Epic = Hidden Reflex, UC Browser = UCWeb; Chrome and Chromium are distinct.
Free software is not necessarily open source; a plugin adds a specialized capability, an extension adds browser features.
Chrome: Ctrl+T new tab, Ctrl+W close tab, Ctrl+Shift+N Incognito; Incognito does not make you anonymous, Tor improves privacy only.
Archie (Alan Emtage), Yahoo (Yang and Filo, 1994), Google (Page and Brin, 1998), Yandex (Russia, 1997), Baidu (China, 2000).
Search engine flow: crawl, index, rank, serve; SERP = results page, SEO = optimization, SEM = marketing.
Surface Web is publicly indexable, Deep Web lies outside ordinary indexes, Dark Web needs special networks such as Tor onion services.
URL = Uniform Resource Locator; DNS looks up IP addresses for names; DHCP gives clients addresses and settings; TCP is reliable, IP is addressing.
Packets can take different routes and vary in length; dial-up is not broadband; cookies live on the client; authentication verifies identity.
